claim: Natural behaviors have redundancy, which implies that humans and animals can achieve their goals with different strategies.
source: Natural behaviors have redundancy, which implies that humans and animals can achieve their goals with different strategies.
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract that sets up the premise of the study.

claim: Both humans and monkeys performed a virtual balancing task under matched experimental conditions.
source: First, both humans and monkeys performed a virtual balancing task for which different control strategies could be utilized. Under matched experimental conditions, corresponding behaviors were observed in humans and monkeys.
evidence: The abstract describes the experimental design where both species performed the same task.

claim: Corresponding behaviors were observed in humans and monkeys under matched experimental conditions.
source: Under matched experimental conditions, corresponding behaviors were observed in humans and monkeys.
evidence: The abstract states that similar behaviors were observed across species.

claim: A generative model was developed that represented two main control objectives to achieve the task goal.
source: Second, a generative model was developed that represented two main control objectives to achieve the task goal.
evidence: The abstract describes the computational modeling approach used in the study.

claim: Model simulations were used to identify aspects of behavior that could distinguish which control objective was being used.
source: Model simulations were used to identify aspects of behavior that could distinguish which control objective was being used.
evidence: The abstract describes how the model was used to make predictions about behavior.

claim: Behavioral signatures allowed inference of the control objective used by human subjects who had been instructed to use one control objective or the other.
source: Third, these behavioral signatures allowed us to infer the control objective used by human subjects who had been instructed to use one control objective or the other.
evidence: The abstract describes validation of the approach using instructed human subjects.

claim: The validated approach allowed inference of control objectives from animal subjects.
source: Based on this validation, we could then infer objectives from animal subjects.
evidence: The abstract states that after validation with humans, the method was applied to animals.

claim: The CST involves balancing an unstable system using horizontal movements of the hand to keep a cursor from moving off the screen.
source: The CST involved balancing an unstable system using horizontal movements of the hand to keep a cursor from moving off the screen (Figure 1A and B).
evidence: The Results section describes the task and references Figure 1.

claim: The cursor dynamics were generated by a linear first-order dynamical system relating hand and cursor kinematics.
source: The cursor dynamics were generated by a linear first-order dynamical system, relating hand and cursor kinematics as described in Quick et al., 2018
evidence: The Results section describes the mathematical model of the task with a citation.

claim: The hand movements were recorded using motion capture with a reflective marker attached to the hand.
source: The hand's displacements were recorded by 3D motion capture (Qualisys, Gothenburg), with a reflective marker attached to the hand.
evidence: The Results section describes the experimental methodology.

claim: The task goal was to keep the cursor within a range of space shown on the screen for a duration of 6 s.
source: The task goal was to keep the cursor within a range of space shown on the screen for a duration of 6 s.
evidence: The Results section describes the task objective.

claim: The task created redundancy in achieving the task goal as there were infinitely many ways to balance the cursor inside the specified region.
source: This created a redundancy in achieving the task goal as there were infinitely many ways in which one could balance the cursor inside the specified region.
evidence: The Results section explains the redundancy inherent in the task.

claim: Two Rhesus monkeys were trained to perform the CST under increasing difficulty levels in a previous study.
source: In a previous study, two Rhesus monkeys were trained to perform the CST under increasing difficulty levels (Quick et al., 2018).
evidence: The Results section references prior work with monkeys.

claim: 18 human subjects were recruited to perform the same task under comparable experimental conditions as the monkeys.
source: Similarly, here 18 human subjects were recruited to perform the same task under comparable experimental conditions as the monkeys (see Methods).
evidence: The Results section describes the human experimental cohort.

claim: There were similarities in performance between humans and monkeys.
source: Overall, there were similarities in performance between humans and monkeys.
evidence: The Results section summarizes comparative findings.

claim: Six human subjects performed the CST with the only instruction to 'perform the task without failing to the best of your ability' in the first experiment.
source: In the first experiment, six human subjects performed the CST with the only instruction to 'perform the task without failing to the best of your ability'.
evidence: The Results section describes Experiment 1 design.

claim: Failure occurred if the cursor escaped the boundaries of the screen (±10 cm from the center) within the trial duration of 6 s.
source: Failure occurred if the cursor escaped the boundaries of the screen (±10 cm from the center) within the trial duration of 6 s.
evidence: The Results section defines the failure criterion.

claim: Subjects received categorical feedback about the outcome at the end of each trial.
source: Subjects received categorical feedback about the outcome at the end of each trial in a text appearing on the screen reading 'Well done!' for success, and 'Failed!' for failure.
evidence: The Results section describes the feedback provided to subjects.

claim: Both humans and monkeys showed a similar pattern of decrease in success rate which was well-captured with a sigmoidal function.
source: Both humans and monkeys showed a similar pattern of decrease in success rate which was well-captured with a sigmoidal function.
evidence: The Results section describes the pattern of success rates across difficulty levels.

claim: The strength of the correlation between cursor and hand movements increased as trials became more challenging in both monkeys and humans, asymptoting towards –1.
source: The strength of the correlation increased as trials became more challenging in both monkeys and humans, asymptoting towards –1.
evidence: The Results section describes how hand-cursor correlation changes with difficulty, referencing Figure 2B.

claim: The RMS ratio showed a gradual decrease as the task difficulty increased for most individuals except Monkey J.
source: Except for Monkey J, the RMS ratio showed a gradual decrease as the task difficulty increased for most individuals.
evidence: The Results section describes the RMS ratio pattern with reference to Figure 2D.

claim: The seemingly divergent behavior of Monkey J was likely due to subject-to-subject variability.
source: The seemingly divergent behavior of Monkey J was likely due to subject-to-subject variability, as also observed in human performers (Appendix 1—figure 1).
evidence: The Results section provides an interpretation of Monkey J's behavior with reference to supplementary data.

claim: As task difficulty increased, subjects tended to respond to cursor displacements faster, more precisely, and more efficiently.
source: Overall, the control metrics presented in Figure 2 give insight into how the CST was performed: as the task difficulty increased, subjects tended to respond to cursor displacements faster (that is, with lower lag), more precisely (seen in the stronger hand-cursor correlation), and more efficiently (with lower RMS ratio).
evidence: The Results section summarizes the findings from the control metrics.

claim: Behavior was comparable between humans and monkeys, suggesting similar control strategies used by both species.
source: Behavior was comparable between humans and monkeys, which suggests that there were similar control strategies used by both species.
evidence: The Results section draws a conclusion about cross-species similarities.

claim: Two types of behavioral patterns appeared recognizable in the data based on single trial observations.
source: Two types of behavioral patterns appeared recognizable in the data.
evidence: The Results section describes qualitative observations of trial-level behavior.

claim: In one behavioral pattern, the cursor seemed to be always balanced around the center of the screen with oscillatory movements.
source: In one case, the cursor seemed to be always balanced around the center of the screen, and any deviations from the center induced a response to bring the cursor back to the center. This was reflected in the oscillatory movements of the cursor around the center, shown in example trials in Figure 1C and D (first row).
evidence: The Results section describes one type of behavioral pattern with reference to Figure 1.

claim: In another behavioral pattern, the cursor either exhibited a slow drift from the center or remained relatively still anywhere within the boundaries.
source: In other trials, the cursor either exhibited a slow drift from the center or remained relatively still anywhere within the boundaries of the screen, with only limited attempts to bring the cursor back to the center (for example, Figure 1C and D, second row).
evidence: The Results section describes a second type of behavioral pattern with reference to Figure 1.

claim: The different patterns of behavior arise from different control objectives, each focused on a different state variable in the state-space of the cursor movement.
source: We hypothesized that these patterns of behavior arise from different control objectives, each focused on a different state variable in the state-space of the cursor movement.
evidence: The Results section presents a hypothesis about the origin of behavioral patterns.

claim: Position Control strategy involves keeping the cursor near the center of the screen as the primary control variable.
source: In the former case, the position of the cursor appeared to be the primary control variable. Under this strategy, subjects might pursue the objective of keeping the cursor near the center of the screen. We refer to this strategy as Position Control.
evidence: The Results section defines the Position Control strategy.

claim: Velocity Control strategy involves slowing down cursor velocity regardless of its position as the primary objective.
source: In the latter case, the cursor velocity seemed to be of primary importance for control, with the objective to slow down cursor velocity regardless of its position in the workspace. We refer to this strategy as Velocity Control.
evidence: The Results section defines the Velocity Control strategy.

claim: A computational approach using a generative model based on optimal feedback control was used to test whether different control strategies could be distinguished by examining behavior.
source: Can we distinguish between different control strategies by examining behavior? To test this idea, we took a computational approach by developing a generative model based on optimal feedback control (Todorov and Jordan, 2002) that could simulate the task under different conditions and with different objectives (Todorov and Jordan, 2002).
evidence: The Results section describes the modeling approach with citations.

claim: The model involved a controller that generated optimal motor commands based on a given objective to perform the CST via a simple effector model.
source: The model involved a controller that generated optimal motor commands based on a given objective to perform the CST via a simple effector model.
evidence: The Results section describes the model architecture.

claim: The model contained a state estimation block that estimated the states of the system based on the given feedback.
source: The model also contained a state estimation block that estimated the states of the system based on the given feedback (Todorov, 2005).
evidence: The Results section describes the state estimation component with citation.

claim: Cursor position and cursor velocity were used as feedback to the controller at each time step.
source: In this case, cursor position and cursor velocity were used as feedback to the controller at each time step.
evidence: The Results section describes the feedback signals in the model.

claim: The control gains were optimally found by minimizing the sum of two cost functions: the cost of effort and the cost of accuracy.
source: The control gains used in the controller to generate the motor commands were optimally found by minimizing the sum of two cost functions: the cost of effort to reduce energy, as well as the cost of accuracy that prevented the states of the system from making large deviations
evidence: The Results section describes the optimization approach in the model.

claim: The simulated trials for Position Control show oscillatory movements of the cursor around the center.
source: As exemplified, the simulated trials for Position Control show oscillatory movements of the cursor around the center, whereas the trials generated based on Velocity Control, exhibited slow drift of the cursor from the center with minimal attempt to correct for such drift.
evidence: The Results section describes the qualitative behavior of model simulations, referencing Figure 3.

claim: The trials generated based on Velocity Control exhibited slow drift of the cursor from the center with minimal attempt to correct for such drift.
source: As exemplified, the simulated trials for Position Control show oscillatory movements of the cursor around the center, whereas the trials generated based on Velocity Control, exhibited slow drift of the cursor from the center with minimal attempt to correct for such drift.
evidence: The Results section describes the qualitative behavior of model simulations, referencing Figure 3.

claim: The simulated characteristics were similar to the observed patterns of behavior in human and monkey data.
source: These characteristics were similar to the observed patterns of behavior in human and monkey data (Figure 1C and D).
evidence: The Results section compares model simulations to empirical data.

claim: For each difficulty level, 500 trials were simulated.
source: For each difficulty level, 500 trials were simulated (see Methods for details).
evidence: The Results section describes the number of simulated trials.

claim: Both simulated control objectives produced similar behavioral characteristics as humans and monkeys at an aggregate level.
source: As shown, for each metric, the model exhibited comparable behavior to the experimental data with regard to the task difficulty: the success rate dropped in a sigmoidal fashion, the strength of the correlation between hand and cursor position increased, and the response lag between hand and cursor as well as the hand/cursor RMS ratio decreased. These results showed that, overall, both simulated control objectives produced similar behavioral characteristics as humans and monkeys.
evidence: The Results section compares model predictions to empirical data, referencing Figure 4A.

claim: The model predicted that Position and Velocity Control performed comparably in success rate and hand-cursor correlation.
source: More interestingly, the model predicted that Position and Velocity Control performed comparably in success rate and hand-cursor correlation (Figure 4A, top two panels), but differed significantly in the response lag and the hand/cursor RMS ratio (Figure 4A, bottom two panels).
evidence: The Results section describes model predictions with reference to Figure 4A.

claim: The model predicted that Position and Velocity Control differed significantly in the response lag and the hand/cursor RMS ratio.
source: More interestingly, the model predicted that Position and Velocity Control performed comparably in success rate and hand-cursor correlation (Figure 4A, top two panels), but differed significantly in the response lag and the hand/cursor RMS ratio (Figure 4A, bottom two panels).
evidence: The Results section describes model predictions with reference to Figure 4A.

claim: Position Control consistently showed larger values for lag and RMS ratio for most task difficulty levels.
source: Specifically, Position Control consistently showed larger values for lag and RMS ratio for most task difficulty levels.
evidence: The Results section describes specific differences between control strategies in the model.

claim: Two new groups of human subjects (n=6 per group) were recruited for Experiment 2.
source: The model indicated that differences in behavioral metrics existed for Position vs Velocity Control. This led to a new experiment for which we recruited two new groups of human subjects (n=6 per group).
evidence: The Results section describes the design of Experiment 2.

claim: Each group in Experiment 2 performed the CST under the same procedure as Experiment 1, except that each group was explicitly instructed to use a specific control objective.
source: Each group performed the CST under the same procedure as described in Experiment 1, except that this time each group was explicitly instructed to use a specific control objective.
evidence: The Results section describes the experimental manipulation in Experiment 2.

claim: One group was asked to perform the task with 'keeping the cursor at the center of the screen at all times' to induce Position Control.
source: One group was asked to perform the task with 'keeping the cursor at the center of the screen at all times'. This instruction intended to induce Position Control.
evidence: The Results section describes the instruction given to one group.

claim: The second group was asked to 'keep the cursor still anywhere within the boundaries of the screen' to induce Velocity Control.
source: The second group was asked to 'keep the cursor still anywhere within the boundaries of the screen'. This instruction aimed to induce Velocity Control (see Methods for details).
evidence: The Results section describes the instruction given to the second group.

claim: The general trends of all four measures with respect to task difficulty in Experiment 2 were consistent with the data generated by the model and the human data from Experiment 1.
source: The general trends of all four measures with respect to the task difficulty were consistent with the data generated by the model, as well as the human data from Experiment 1 (Figure 2).
evidence: The Results section compares Experiment 2 data to model and Experiment 1 data, referencing Figure 4B.

claim: The behavioral differences between the two control strategies in human data matched the predictions of the model relatively well.
source: Importantly, the behavioral differences between the two control strategies in human data matched the predictions of the model relatively well (Figure 4A and B)
evidence: The Results section compares human data to model predictions.

claim: The group with Position Control instruction showed a significantly larger hand-cursor lag compared to the group with Velocity Control instructions.
source: the group with Position Control instruction showed a significantly larger hand-cursor lag (unpaired t-test: t10=3.79, p=0.004) and hand/cursor RMS ratio (unpaired t-test: t10=5.27, p<10–3) compared to the group with Velocity Control instructions (Figure 4C).
evidence: The Results section reports statistical comparison between groups with reference to Figure 4C.

claim: The group with Position Control instruction showed a significantly larger hand/cursor RMS ratio compared to the group with Velocity Control instructions.
source: the group with Position Control instruction showed a significantly larger hand-cursor lag (unpaired t-test: t10=3.79, p=0.004) and hand/cursor RMS ratio (unpaired t-test: t10=5.27, p<10–3) compared to the group with Velocity Control instructions (Figure 4C).
evidence: The Results section reports statistical comparison between groups with reference to Figure 4C.

claim: The model captured the overall performance features observed in the data and successfully demonstrated the redundancy of control strategies in CST performance.
source: These results showed that the model not only captured the overall performance features observed in the data, it also successfully demonstrated the redundancy of control strategies in CST performance.
evidence: The Results section summarizes the model validation findings.

claim: The model could qualitatively distinguish between control strategies at an aggregate level of performance.
source: Importantly, it could qualitatively distinguish between such strategies at an aggregate level of performance.
evidence: The Results section describes the model's capability.

claim: Two metrics were defined that captured the state-space behavior of the cursor in each trial.
source: To further investigate what control objective was preferred by an individual or in a given trial, we examined the predictions of the model about the cursor behavior in state space, and then tested these predictions using experimental data from Experiment 2. Two metrics were defined that captured the state-space behavior of the cursor in each trial.
evidence: The Results section describes the development of new metrics.

claim: For Position Control, all trials scattered around the origin of the state space, whereas for Velocity Control, they could deviate from the origin.
source: It was expected that for Position Control, all trials scattered around the origin of the state space, whereas for Velocity Control, they could deviate from the origin.
evidence: The Results section describes expected differences between control strategies.

claim: Position Control resulted in a distribution with little correlation between cursor position and its velocity, closely scattered around the center.
source: As shown, the distribution of trials in this space differed markedly between the two control objectives (also see Appendix 1—figures 2 and 3). Position Control resulted in a distribution with little correlation between cursor position and its velocity, and closely scattered around the center.
evidence: The Results section describes model predictions with reference to Figure 5A.

claim: Velocity Control revealed an elongated distribution with a relatively strong correlation between the cursor position and its velocity.
source: In contrast, Velocity Control revealed an elongated distribution with a relatively strong correlation between the cursor position and its velocity.
evidence: The Results section describes model predictions with reference to Figure 5A.

claim: Sensitivity analyses showed that different magnitudes of noise and delay only affected the success rates, but no other features.
source: We further examined whether such distinction in behavior was solely due to a change in the control objective, or whether varying other parameters in the model simulations, such as motor noise, delay, or effort cost, could also generate similar distinctive patterns. These sensitivity analyses showed that different magnitudes of noise and delay only affected the success rates, but no other features, as to be expected.
evidence: The Results section describes sensitivity analyses with reference to supplementary figures.

claim: Effort cost could not account for the observed differences in movement distributions.
source: Effort cost also could not account for the observed differences in the above mentioned movement distributions (Appendix 1—figures 4–6).
evidence: The Results section describes sensitivity analyses with reference to supplementary figures.

claim: Subjects in the Velocity Control group showed significantly larger correlations than individuals in the Position Control group.
source: As shown, overall, subjects in the Velocity Control group showed significantly larger correlations than individuals in the Position Control group (unpaired t-test on the Pearson correlation coefficient: t10=4.06, p=0.002).
evidence: The Results section reports statistical comparison between groups with reference to Figure 5C.

claim: When grouping the trials into easy and moderate difficulty trials, the cursor position and velocity relations did not change and the correlations for the two control objectives continued to reveal the same relative difference.
source: When grouping the trials into easy and moderate difficulty trials, the cursor position and velocity relations did not change and the correlations for the two control objectives continued to reveal the same relative difference between the control objectives (see Appendix 1—figures 7 and 8).
evidence: The Results section describes additional analyses with reference to supplementary figures.

claim: The control objective may not be fixed for an individual throughout their performance and might vary from one trial to the next due to the task's redundancy.
source: Due to the task's redundancy, the control objective may not be fixed for an individual throughout their performance and might vary from one trial to the next.
evidence: The Results section discusses the possibility of trial-to-trial variability in control objectives.

claim: The magnitude of cursor movement was calculated as the root mean squared (RMS) of its position and velocity in each trial.
source: To this end, we examined the magnitude of cursor movement calculated as the root mean squared (RMS) of its position and velocity in each trial.
evidence: The Results section describes a new metric for single-trial analysis.

claim: Position Control aimed to minimize the RMS of cursor position, while Velocity Control aimed to minimize the RMS of cursor velocity.
source: This was directly related to the cost functions used in the model (Equation 2), which provided a more direct comparison regarding the primacy of Position versus Velocity Control of the cursor: Position Control aimed to minimize the RMS of cursor position, while Velocity Control aimed to minimize the RMS of cursor velocity.
evidence: The Results section explains the relationship between the RMS metric and control objectives.

claim: For Position Control, the distribution of trials leans towards the vertical axis, whereas for Velocity Control, it leans mainly towards the horizontal axis.
source: For Position Control, the distribution of trials leans towards the vertical axis (restricting cursor position but allowing large cursor velocities), whereas for Velocity Control, it leans mainly towards the horizontal axis (a larger range of cursor positions but restricted velocities).
evidence: The Results section describes model predictions with reference to Figure 6A.

claim: The distinction between control objectives could be quantified by the slope of a fitted regression line to the data, with relatively larger slopes indicating Position Control and smaller slopes signaling Velocity Control.
source: This distinction could be quantified by the slope of a fitted regression line to the data, with relatively larger slopes indicating Position Control and smaller slopes signaling Velocity Control.
evidence: The Results section describes how to quantify control objectives using regression slopes.

claim: Similar patterns of behavior could be observed in the human data from Experiment 2 as illustrated in Figure 6B and C.
source: Similar patterns of behavior could be observed in the human data from Experiment 2 as illustrated in Figure 6B and C
evidence: The Results section compares model predictions to empirical data.

claim: The Position Control group showed significantly larger regression slope than the Velocity Control group.
source: with the Position Control group showing significantly larger regression slope than the Velocity Control group (unpaired t-test, t10=6.33, p<0.001).
evidence: The Results section reports statistical comparison between groups with reference to Figure 6C.

claim: The regression slope could more clearly distinguish between individual trials than could the correlation coefficient metric regarding their corresponding control objective.
source: The regression slope could more clearly distinguish between individual trials than could the correlation coefficient metric shown in Figure 5, regarding their corresponding control objective
evidence: The Results section compares the discriminative power of different metrics.

claim: A support vector machine classifier was trained using simulation results based on the cursor movement in its RMS space.
source: To achieve the goal of inferring an individual's control objective based on their performance, we used the control characteristics that our computational approach introduced to distinguish between different control objectives. To this end, the simulation results based on the cursor movement in its RMS space (Figure 6A) were used to train a simple classifier, a support vector machine (see Methods).
evidence: The Results section describes the classification approach.

claim: The classifier determined whether a given trial was likely performed as Position Control or Velocity Control based on learned regression slopes from the RMS distributions.
source: This classifier then determined, based on the learned regression slopes from the RMS distributions (Figure 7A), whether a given trial was likely performed as Position Control, or Velocity Control.
evidence: The Results section describes how the classifier works.

claim: The classifier was trained on synthetic data generated with Position and Velocity Control (2250 trials each).
source: We first evaluated the accuracy of the classifier based on simulated data, where the classifier was trained on synthetic data generated with Position and Velocity Control (2250 trials each), and then tested on a separate set of trials from either control objective (2500 trials).
evidence: The Results section describes the classifier training and testing procedure.

claim: For any given trial, the classifier obtained a posterior probability indicating to what extent that trial was generated under Position Control.
source: For any given trial, the classifier obtained a posterior probability indicating to what extent that trial was generated under Position Control.
evidence: The Results section describes the classifier output.

claim: The probability of 95% and higher identified the given trial as Position Control, while the probability less than 5% labeled the trial as Velocity Control.
source: The probability of 95% and higher identified the given trial as Position Control, while the probability less than 5% labeled the trial as Velocity Control; anything in between was considered 'Uncertain' as to the underlying control objective.
evidence: The Results section describes the classification thresholds.

claim: 6.2% of trials that were generated with Position Control were misclassified as Velocity Control.
source: The results showed that 6.2% of trials that were generated with Position Control were misclassified as Velocity Control, and 5.5% of trials that were generated with Velocity Control were misclassified as Position Control.
evidence: The Results section reports classifier accuracy on simulated data.

claim: 5.5% of trials that were generated with Velocity Control were misclassified as Position Control.
source: The results showed that 6.2% of trials that were generated with Position Control were misclassified as Velocity Control, and 5.5% of trials that were generated with Velocity Control were misclassified as Position Control.
evidence: The Results section reports classifier accuracy on simulated data.

claim: For the Position Control group, most of the trials were rightfully classified as Position Control.
source: As shown in Figure 7B, for the Position Control group, most of the trials were rightfully classified as Position Control, and similarly for the Velocity Control group, the majority of trials were classified as Velocity Control.
evidence: The Results section reports classifier performance on human data with reference to Figure 7B.

claim: For the Velocity Control group, the majority of trials were classified as Velocity Control.
source: As shown in Figure 7B, for the Position Control group, most of the trials were rightfully classified as Position Control, and similarly for the Velocity Control group, the majority of trials were classified as Velocity Control.
evidence: The Results section reports classifier performance on human data with reference to Figure 7B.

claim: The classifier correctly determined the control strategy of each individual without being trained on any experimental data.
source: This showed that the classifier correctly determined the control strategy of each individual without being trained on any experimental data.
evidence: The Results section summarizes the classifier validation with reference to Figure 7C.

claim: The classifier was used to determine what control objective was used in each trial for humans who received no instructions and for monkeys.
source: The ultimate test of our approach would be to infer the control strategy used by individuals whose control objective was unknown, that is the monkeys and the humans who received no instructions about the control strategy in Experiment 1. After representing the performance of each subject in the RMS space, the classifier was used to determine what control objective was used in each trial.
evidence: The Results section describes application of the classifier to uninstructed subjects.

claim: Human subject NI-S2 more likely adopted Velocity Control.
source: For example, human subject NI-S2 more likely adopted Velocity Control, while human subject NI-S4 mainly performed the task with Position Control (Figure 8B).
evidence: The Results section reports inferred control objectives for specific subjects with reference to Figure 8B.

claim: Human subject NI-S4 mainly performed the task with Position Control.
source: For example, human subject NI-S2 more likely adopted Velocity Control, while human subject NI-S4 mainly performed the task with Position Control (Figure 8B).
evidence: The Results section reports inferred control objectives for specific subjects with reference to Figure 8B.

claim: Monkey I seemed to prefer Velocity Control.
source: Similarly, Monkey I seemed to prefer Velocity Control, while Monkey J most likely adopted Position Control (Figure 8C).
evidence: The Results section reports inferred control objectives for monkeys with reference to Figure 8C.

claim: Monkey J most likely adopted Position Control.
source: Similarly, Monkey I seemed to prefer Velocity Control, while Monkey J most likely adopted Position Control (Figure 8C).
evidence: The Results section reports inferred control objectives for monkeys with reference to Figure 8C.

claim: The procedure enabled inference of the underlying control objective at a single trial level and identification of which objective was overall preferred by humans and monkeys when no explicit knowledge about their strategy was available.
source: Ultimately, our procedure enabled us to not only infer the underlying control objective at a single trial level, but also identify which objective was overall preferred by humans and monkeys when no explicit knowledge about their strategy was available.
evidence: The Results section summarizes the capabilities of the approach.

claim: The CST was challenging and exhibited different ways to achieve task success.
source: In a matching task design, humans and monkeys performed a virtual balancing task, where they controlled an unstable system using lateral movements of their right hand to keep a cursor on the screen. The task was challenging and, importantly, exhibited different ways to achieve task success.
evidence: The Discussion section summarizes key features of the task.

claim: The task required skill that was nevertheless simple enough for monkeys to learn and ultimately achieve the same level of proficiency as humans.
source: The task required skill that was nevertheless simple enough for monkeys to learn and ultimately achieve the same level of proficiency as humans.
evidence: The Discussion section describes the task's suitability for comparative studies.

claim: Studies in motor neurophysiology have largely relied on simple paradigms such as center-out movements.
source: Studies in motor neurophysiology have largely relied on simple paradigms such as center-out movements (Batista et al., 1999; Cisek et al., 2003; Georgopoulos et al., 1986; Pruszynski et al., 2011; Scott and Kalaska, 1997), which were brief in duration, highly stereotypical across repetitions, and could be performed to a reasonable degree of success with limited sensory feedback.
evidence: The Discussion section describes the state of the field with citations.

claim: Simple paradigms were needed to make sense of noisy neural data through averaging trials over many repeats of highly similar behaviors.
source: Such characteristics were needed to make sense of noisy neural data through averaging trials over many repeats of highly similar behaviors.
evidence: The Discussion section explains the rationale for simple paradigms.

claim: Constrained behaviors are not common in natural settings, where we continually utilize sensory feedback to respond to our environment.
source: However, such constrained behaviors are not common in natural settings, where we continually utilize sensory feedback to respond to our environment, interact with objects around us, and never do the same action the exact same way.
evidence: The Discussion section contrasts laboratory tasks with natural behavior.

claim: The CST continuously engages feedback-driven control mechanisms for a prolonged period of time and is rich in its trial-to-trial and subject-to-subject variability.
source: The task employed here, the CST, continuously engages feedback-driven control mechanisms for a prolonged period of time and is rich in its trial-to-trial and subject-to-subject variability.
evidence: The Discussion section describes advantages of the CST.

claim: Both monkeys and humans can learn the CST and their behavior can be studied and modeled due to the ability to titrate task difficulty.
source: As we can titrate the difficulty of the task, both monkeys and humans can learn it and we can study and model their behavior.
evidence: The Discussion section describes the advantages of the CST for comparative studies.

claim: In the eye movement literature, comparisons between features in monkeys and humans have been more common.
source: In the eye movement literature, comparisons between features in monkeys and humans have been more common (e.g. Dorris et al., 2000; Groh and Sparks, 1996).
evidence: The Discussion section provides context about comparative studies with citations.

claim: Experimental findings in primates have been instrumental to understanding impairments in eye movement control in humans.
source: In fact, experimental findings in primates have been instrumental to understanding impairments in eye movement control in humans.
evidence: The Discussion section discusses the value of primate research.

claim: Direct comparative studies conducted in different laboratories with exact matches between experimental conditions are harder to achieve.
source: Direct comparative studies conducted in different laboratories with exact matches between experimental conditions are harder to achieve.
evidence: The Discussion section discusses challenges in comparative research.

claim: In an earlier attempt of modeling CST, a simple PD controller with delay in sensory feedback was proposed to explain the recorded behavior.
source: In an earlier attempt of modeling CST, a simple PD controller with delay in sensory feedback was proposed to explain the recorded behavior (Quick et al., 2018).
evidence: The Discussion section references prior modeling work with citation.

claim: The earlier PD controller model was limited in its ability to capture most features observed in the data, such as success rate or correlation between hand and cursor position.
source: However, the model was limited in its ability to capture most features observed in the data, such as success rate or correlation between hand and cursor position.
evidence: The Discussion section critiques prior modeling work.

claim: Optimal feedback control (OFC) has been introduced as an effective approach to understanding the control mechanisms of reaching movements at the level of behavior.
source: In the past years, optimal feedback control (OFC) has been introduced as an effective approach to understanding the control mechanisms of reaching movements at the level of behavior (Diedrichsen et al., 2010; McNamee and Wolpert, 2019; Pruszynski and Scott, 2012; Scott, 2004; Todorov, 2004)
evidence: The Discussion section discusses the OFC framework with citations.

claim: OFC has been applied separately in human research and monkey research.
